description: The Hungry Void earns its name ironically—rather than consuming, it rejects everything that approaches. The region registers on gravitational sensors as a zone of negative mass, pushing rather than pulling, repelling rather than attracting. Debris that drifts nearby accelerates away, creating a visible halo of ejected matter around an empty core. Light itself bends outward, creating an inverted gravitational lens that makes stars behind the void appear to scatter rather than compress. The effect is deeply counterintuitive, violating expectations built on a lifetime of normal physics.

Entering the Hungry Void requires constant thrust against the repulsive force, fuel consumption increasing exponentially as ships penetrate deeper. The central region has never been reached—the force becomes overwhelming long before any vessel achieves core proximity. Objects released within are ejected with startling velocity; the probe Archimedes reached relativistic speeds simply by being let go. This property has obvious applications for those creative enough to harness it, essentially a natural mass driver of unprecedented power.

No natural process should create negative gravity. Exotic matter with negative mass is theoretically possible but has never been detected elsewhere. The Hungry Void's existence suggests either unknown physics or artificial creation, though no creator has been identified. The void shows no signs of decay or change; whatever maintains the negative field appears stable indefinitely. Some researchers propose it's a remnant of the early universe, when conditions allowed exotic matter formation. Others suspect more recent and purposeful origin.

The Hungry Void currently serves as a research site and occasional weapon test facility—the ejection velocity makes it useful for accelerating projectiles without propellant. Military strategists have proposed using it as a defensive position, noting that attacking vessels must fight the field itself to approach. The scientific community remains more interested in understanding how negative mass exists at all. If the mechanism could be replicated, the implications for propulsion and energy generation would be revolutionary. For now, the void keeps its secrets, pushing away all who seek to uncover them.
